analysis.one_liner: Lets safety regulators override company-chosen fixes for dangerous products and removes the cap on civil fines.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on June 29, 2000, drew no cosponsors, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, when a company sells a product the Consumer Product Safety Commission finds unsafe, the company gets to pick its own remedy: repair it, replace it, or refund buyers. This bill would let the Commission override that choice and order whichever action actually protects the public. It would also raise the fine for each safety violation from $5,000 to $7,000, delete the $1.25 million ceiling on fines for a related series of violations, and lengthen prison time for executives who knowingly or repeatedly violate product safety law.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy defective or hazardous products. When a company's chosen fix — say, a repair — doesn't actually make a dangerous product safe, the Commission could order a stronger remedy like a refund or replacement. Higher, uncapped fines and criminal exposure for repeat violations would give companies a stronger reason to catch safety problems before products reach store shelves.

how_it_helps.text: Lets the Commission order a different remedy (repair, replacement, or refund) whenever the action a manufacturer chose is not in the public interest, after an informal hearing [S2][S3].
Raises the civil penalty per violation from $5,000 to $7,000 and removes the $1.25 million cap on total fines for a related series of violations, with inflation adjustments [S2][S3].

Raises criminal penalties: up to 1 year in prison for knowing violations and up to 3 years for knowing and willful violations, and treats a company's second or subsequent violation as knowing and willful [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers, distributors, and retailers of consumer products, who would face larger and potentially unlimited civil fines, tougher criminal exposure for repeat violations, and less control over how they resolve recalls and safety defects. Some of those costs could be passed to consumers in prices, though that trade is the point of the bill: making unsafe products more expensive to sell.

drawbacks.text: Companies would lose control over how they respond to safety defects, and the Commission could impose remedies a business considers disproportionate, adding litigation and compliance costs [S3].
Removing the cap on civil penalties means a single ongoing problem could stack fines without limit, a burden that weighs heaviest on smaller firms with thinner margins [S3].
Stronger penalties raise costs that some businesses would pass along in prices, so consumers pay partly at the register for safety enforcement they benefit from elsewhere [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to anyone who buys products covered by federal safety rules; the costs fall mainly on the companies selling them, and only when they violate safety law in the first place. The main honest caveat is that fines and recall remedies are blunt tools, and uncapped penalties plus mandatory hearings could make the Commission slow and heavy-handed. On balance this is a modest, targeted strengthening of existing enforcement rather than a rewrite, but it was never debated, so its design was never tested by committee scrutiny.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Hollings introduced the bill on June 29, 2000, 'by request' — a phrase that signals introduction on behalf of an outside requester, typically the administration — and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S3][S5].
The bill drew zero cosponsors in its six months of life [S4].
No further action of any kind appears in the record after the committee referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote took place before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and retailers of consumer products are better off: with the bill dead, they kept the right to choose their own recall remedies and the $1.25 million cap on civil fines stayed in place.

for.name: Sen. Ernest Hollings
for.role: U.S. Senator from South Carolina (ranking Democrat, Senate Commerce Committee)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill by request on June 29, 2000 and delivered introductory remarks; the record shows no other sponsor action.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no other senator cosponsored, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never recorded.

industries.industry: Consumer product manufacturers, distributors, and retailers
industries.note: The bill would remove their control over choosing recall remedies, raise per-violation fines from $5,000 to $7,000, lift the $1.25 million cap on related-series penalties, and extend criminal liability to repeat offenders. The industry's interest in keeping penalties low and remedies company-controlled runs against the bill's consumer-safety purpose. Sources: [S2][S3].
